analysis.one_liner: Requires police and intelligence agencies to get a judge's warrant before using cell-site simulators to track phones.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced July 29, 2025 by Rep. Ted Lieu with one Republican cosponsor and sent to four House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Cell-site simulators (often called Stingrays) are devices that impersonate a cell tower to locate phones and intercept transmissions — including phones of bystanders who are not targets. This bill would make it a federal offense, with fines up to $250,000, to use one in the United States without a warrant from a judge, with narrow exceptions for true emergencies, foreign intelligence surveillance under FISA, prison contraband screening, and equipment testing. It would also bar evidence gathered illegally from court, let victims sue for damages, require police to notify people whose phones were swept up, and force agencies to report their use to Congress each year.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who carries a cell phone. The bill's warrant requirement, notification rules, and minimization procedures protect innocent bystanders whose phones get swept up when police point a simulator at a neighborhood, and its exclusionary rule and private right of action give people remedies when agencies ignore the rules.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any individual or entity to knowingly use a cell-site simulator in the United States, except under the bill's narrow exceptions, with a fine of up to $250,000 for violations.

Allows law enforcement to use a simulator only with a warrant that shows other methods failed or are too dangerous, specifies the narrowest possible area and time of operation, and expires within 30 days.

Bars information gathered through unlawful simulator use, and evidence derived from it, from being used in any court or government proceeding, and gives targets a civil action for damages and injunctive relief.
Requires judges to be told whether the device could disrupt 911 calls, suicide-hotline calls, or other communications, and requires notice to people whose devices the government swept up.

Requires the Justice, Homeland Security, Defense, and Intelligence Community inspectors general to report annually and publicly on how often simulators were used, how many bystander devices were collected, and how many bystanders' data was not destroyed.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement and intelligence agencies would lose the ability to track phones without a judge's approval, and simulator makers would face a new testing and certification regime. Taxpayers indirectly bear the cost of the warrant process and annual reporting.

drawbacks.text: The emergency exception lets agencies use a simulator without a warrant and apply for one up to 48 hours later, and exceptions for FISA surveillance, Secret Service protective duties, and prison contraband screening leave substantial carve-outs to the warrant requirement.

The warrant process — showing other methods failed, certifying the narrowest scope, and third-party testing of the device model — could add delay in urgent investigations, which is the standard objection from law enforcement, and the bill gives agencies two years (three for existing device models) before the rules take effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real but modest: a judge's sign-off and narrow-scoping requirements add friction to a surveillance tool that has historically been used without warrants and sweeps in bystanders' phones. The bill keeps emergency, FISA, prison, and testing pathways open, so legitimate uses survive; the cost is some procedural delay, and the benefit is that millions of phone owners stop being trackable on an agency's discretion alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to four House committees, and none of them has taken it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the Cell-Site Simulator Warrant Act of 2025 in the House on July 29, 2025, joined by Republican Rep. Tom McClintock.
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and, additionally, to the Intelligence, Armed Services, and Energy and Commerce committees.
No committee has held a hearing or markup, and the bill has received no floor action since introduction.
The bill would create the first comprehensive federal statutory framework for cell-site simulator use, which is currently governed mainly by agency policies rather than statute.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, law enforcement and intelligence agencies, which keep their current ability to use cell-site simulators without any statutory warrant requirement.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan at the member level — a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — but with only two supporters and no committee action from either party, the parties' positions are untested.

industries.note: The bill ends their ability to point a cell-site simulator at a neighborhood without a judge's warrant, forces them to disclose disruption risks, notify swept-up bystanders, destroy non-target data, and face lawsuits and evidence exclusion for violations. Their interest in unchecked tracking runs directly against the phone privacy of ordinary people.

A warrant requirement and disclosure rules could shrink untracked use, but the bill also writes simulator use into statute as a lawful, regulated practice and requires third-party FCC-accredited lab certification of each model — a compliance requirement that formalizes the market and gives existing models a three-year runway.

Simulators can degrade or block phone service, including 911 calls; the bill forces warrant applications to disclose those risks and certify the device model was independently tested, which protects the service carriers sell and customers rely on.

analysis.trajectory: A privacy bill referred to four committees with two sponsors rarely gets standalone action. Its most realistic paths forward are as an amendment to a larger vehicle, such as FISA reauthorization or a defense bill, or reintroduction in a future Congress; on its own, it will likely sit until the session ends.
